local_support.anchor_text: gif hīe him gefultumoden ... oferwinnan
local_support.learner_help: Gefultumoden is a preterite subjunctive: if they, the Romans, would help them, the Britons. local_support.title: Opening passive and proportion
local_support.text: Ymbseald means surrounded/beset; mid introduces the surrounding dangers. Efne reinforces the assertion. The paired swā clauses with comparatives mean the greater the worldly dignities, the fiercer the dangers. This proportional construction remains supported, distinct from prior equal-degree swā…swā.
local_support.display_obligation: Print this exact support beside the assigned task or reading and keep it visible during assessment; no unsupported recall is required.

local_support.title: Examples recognized and understood
local_support.text: Be ðǣm is a separate dative prepositional phrase, by/from that: it points back to the preceding proposition as the basis for inference. Bȳsena is the accusative examples governed by the two modal infinitives oncnāwan and ongietan. The paired verbs reinforce one act of understanding; do not treat bȳsena as dative because be appears earlier.
local_support.display_obligation: Print this exact support beside the assigned task or reading and keep it visible during assessment; no unsupported recall is required.

local_support.title: Tree, growth, result and reflexive
local_support.text: The relative ðe identifies the tree. Wiexð is the exact source third singular grows, beside the earlier selected wiext. The result clause ðæt hit hlīfað explains how it grows: so that it towers above the other trees. Brǣt hit means spreads itself; this hit is accusative and refers to the same tree. The first hit in the result clause is its nominative subject.
local_support.display_obligation: Print this exact support beside the assigned task or reading and keep it visible during assessment; no unsupported recall is required.

local_support.title: Storm and passive comparison
local_support.text: Sęmninga is suddenly. Gestęnt is singular present, assails/comes on; Cook’s note identifies storm and the following strong wind as its two subjects. Preserve the singular Old English wording; idiomatic English can use plural strike. The two following ðonne tokens function differently: then in the temporal correlation and than after swīðlicor more violently. Gewǣged and geswęnged are supplied passive bases. Se ōðer wudu means the rest of the forest, as the original note says.
local_support.display_obligation: Print this exact support beside the assigned task or reading and keep it visible during assessment; no unsupported recall is required.

local_support.title: Original157n3: hruron
local_support.text: Cook asks for the indicative preterite plural of hrēosan. Supply hruron (all plural persons); the classII plural uses u with s/r alternation. This is reference-only help, not a new complete productive hrēosan paradigm or an unaided recall task.
local_support.display_obligation: Print this exact support beside the assigned task or reading and keep it visible during assessment; no unsupported recall is required.

local_support.title: Cliffs and coordinated infinitives
local_support.text: Swā bið ēac gelīce be… means it is likewise also with/concerning…. The plural hīe refers to the cliffs/crags. Hlīfiað means tower and feorr ūp far up. Onginnað begin governs both feallan and hrēosan; full strengthens ðearlice, very violently. The two fall verbs can reinforce one collapse rather than name two chronologically separate events. Tō eorðan gives the destination to the earth.
local_support.display_obligation: Print this exact support beside the assigned task or reading and keep it visible during assessment; no unsupported recall is required.

local_support.title: ðā-ðe
local_support.text: Ðā-ðe is the exact joined source spelling of plural relative ðā with ðe, which. It is nominative plural as subject of standað and refers to muntum and dūnum. The prior compound-relative construction is reused with this explicitly supplied spelling; no new headword or unrestricted joining rule is inferred.

local_support.title: Mountains and punishment
local_support.text: Supply the repeated it is likewise with/concerning after Swilce ēac. Hēah is adverbial high with standað. Ðā-hwæðre means nevertheless. The mountains pay the penalty of their pre-eminence: the ðæt-clause explains that penalty. Geneahhe is often, preserving the source’s unmarked spelling beside dictionary genēahhe. Geðrēade, geðrǣste and geslægene are agreeing plural passive participles: punished/battered/struck by heavenly fire and thunderbolts. These exact forms do not assign three full new paradigms.

local_support.title: The human conclusion
local_support.text: The first subject is the high powers; hrēosað and feallað reinforce their fall, and weorðað tō lore means come to destruction. The second subject is the wealth of this world, which becomes sorrow (tō sorge). The third is these earthly wonders, which come to nothing (tō nāhte). The tō-result expressions are supplied; they are not instances of the earlier nominative-predicate become frame.

local_support.text: The two superlative adverbs mean “most clearly and most intelligibly.” For plus dative introduces the worldly cares that constrained how clearly Alfred could explain it. local_support.text: Ælfred is subject. The feminine hīe/hēo refers to bōc. The source-language phrases use of plus dative; on Englisc gives the translation’s goal. Word be worde contrasts literal verbal correspondence with andgiet of andgiete, sense for sense. Gedōn describes the work’s resulting arrangement.

local_support.text: The two superlative adverbs mean “most clearly and most intelligibly.” For plus dative introduces the worldly cares that constrained how clearly Alfred could explain it. Ǣgðer ge ... ge means “both ... and.” On mōde/on līchaman identify mind and body. Sind is the plural present “are.” The relative ðe at word61 refers to bisga; those cares are the subject of becōmon.
local_support.origin_category: new teaching material explaining exact source
local_support.display_obligation: Keep this exact help visible beside every assigned task and during its assessment; no independent recall of supplied material is tested.

local_support.text: Hæfde underfangen = “had received/taken charge of.” The repeated hæfde governs both geleornod and gewęnd: “had studied ... and translated ...”. Ðēah here is “nevertheless”; ðā ... ðā frames “when ... then.” Tō Engliscum spelle and tō lēoðe mark resulting literary form. Hīe/hēo still refers to the book.
local_support.origin_category: new teaching material explaining exact source
local_support.display_obligation: Keep this exact help visible beside every assigned task and during its assessment; no independent recall of supplied material is tested.

local_support.text: Supply hē (Alfred) with bitt and hālsað, as Cook’s note4 directs. Ǣlcne ðāra ðe ... means “each of those who ...”. Lyste is impersonal: “whom it may please to read this book”; its understood accusative experiencer is the prospective reader. The requested ðæt clause contains subjunctive gebidde, “that he pray for him.”

local_support.text: Ne wīte continues the request: “and not blame him.” In gif hē hit rihtlicor ongiete ðonne hē meahte, the first hē is the reader and the second is Alfred (Cook’s notes6–7). Ongiete is subjunctive; wīte is the verb “blame,” not the noun “punishment.”

local_support.text: Be ... mǣðe and be ... ǣmettan mean according to the measure of one’s understanding and one’s available leisure. Sceal governs sprecan and dōn. Both ðæt ... and ðæt-ðæt ... function as “what/that which.” Preserve the source’s hyphenated spelling in the latter.

local_support.text: Ælfred is subject. The feminine hīe/hēo refers to bōc. The source-language phrases use of plus dative; on Englisc gives the translation’s goal. local_support.text: The two superlative adverbs mean “most clearly and most intelligibly.” For plus dative introduces the worldly cares that constrained how clearly Alfred could explain it. Ǣgðer ge ... ge means “both ... and.” On mōde/on līchaman identify mind and body. Sind is the plural present “are.” The relative ðe at word61 refers to bisga; those cares are the subject of becōmon.

local_support.text: Hæfde underfangen = “had received/taken charge of.” The repeated hæfde governs both geleornod and gewęnd: “had studied ... and translated ...”. local_support.text: The for phrases name grounds of appeal. In ðǣre hālgan rōde tācne, the genitive phrase “of the holy cross” depends on dative tācne. Sanctæ Marian and Sancti Michaeles are supplied names in genitive function with mixed foreign-name inflection; do not derive a new productive Latin paradigm. Gehīersumnesse is obedience. Hālgena means saints; lufan is the weak noun’s dative; earnungum means merits.

local_support.text: The requested ðæt clause has gewissie, “that you guide.” Bęt ðonne ic āworhte tō ðē means better than my conduct towards you has deserved. The following gewissa is a direct singular command. In mīnre sāwle ðearfe, mīnre sāwle is genitive, dependent on dative ðearfe: “for my soul’s benefit.” Cunne is first-singular subjunctive, “than I myself may know.”

local_support.text: Gestaðela, gestranga, āfierr and gescield are addressed singular commands. The latter adjectives agree with dative plural wiðerwinnum.

local_support.text: The for phrases name grounds of appeal. In ðǣre hālgan rōde tācne, the genitive phrase “of the holy cross” depends on dative tācne. Hālgena means saints; lufan is the weak noun’s dative; earnungum means merits.

local_support.text: The requested ðæt clause has gewissie, “that you guide.” Bęt ðonne ic āworhte tō ðē means better than my conduct towards you has deserved. local_support.text: The for phrases name grounds of appeal. In ðǣre hālgan rōde tācne, the genitive phrase “of the holy cross” depends on dative tācne. Sanctæ Marian and Sancti Michaeles are supplied names in genitive function with mixed foreign-name inflection; do not derive a new productive Latin paradigm. Gehīersumnesse is obedience. local_support.text: The requested ðæt clause has gewissie, “that you guide.” Bęt ðonne ic āworhte tō ðē means better than my conduct towards you has deserved. The following gewissa is a direct singular command. In mīnre sāwle ðearfe, mīnre sāwle is genitive, dependent on dative ðearfe: “for my soul’s benefit.” Cunne is first-singular subjunctive, “than I myself may know.”

local_support.text: Gestaðela, gestranga, āfierr and gescield are addressed singular commands. The latter adjectives agree with dative plural wiðerwinnum.

local_support.title: A hundredfold requital
local_support.text: Use him mid hundtēontigum forgolden bið, “he will be repaid a hundredfold,” with the finite verb last.
